title: Two Leaders, One Big Meeting: Trump and Xi Talk AI, Trade, and Taiwan
summary:
Imagine two of the most powerful leaders in the world sitting down at the White House. That's what happened when President Trump hosted China's leader, Xi Jinping. It was Xi's first trip to Washington in more than 10 years!

There was a big military welcome on the South Lawn. Then the two leaders held two meetings. Later, Trump and the First Lady planned a fancy State Dinner.

So what did they talk about? Four big things: trade, technology, Taiwan, and Iran.

On trade, the U.S. and China agreed to keep their 'trade truce' — a deal where the U.S. won't raise tariffs (taxes on goods from other countries) and China keeps selling rare earth magnets. Those tiny magnets are inside cell phones, electric cars, and even F-35 fighter jets. China makes almost all of them.

On technology, the two countries are starting a new U.S.-China AI Dialogue. That means they'll talk about keeping AI safe. Xi said AI should 'always be under human control.'

Taiwan and Iran also came up. A U.S. official said America has not sent a second weapons package to Taiwan because China might send more weapons to Iran in return.

Both sides seem to want one thing: stability — keeping things calm.
why_it_matters: Your phone, tablet, or family car is full of parts that travel between the U.S. and China, so when these two countries argue or agree on taxes and technology, it can change prices in your family's shopping cart and even which gadgets you can buy.

background_read: The White House (the U.S. president's home and office in Washington, D.C.) is where leaders hold grand events like a State Dinner, a very fancy official meal for an important visitor.

Rare earth magnets are made with special metals, and China is the world's biggest maker of them, which is why many countries depend on China for the tiny magnets inside phones, cars, and military planes.

Taiwan (an island off China's coast that has its own government) has been a subject of disagreement between the U.S. and China for many decades, and the U.S. has sold weapons to Taiwan, which makes China angry.
The United States and China are the world's two largest economies. They are rivals, but they also buy and sell huge amounts of goods to each other, so a trade truce helps both sides.
Article_Structure: WHO: President Trump, China's leader Xi Jinping, the First Lady, and a U.S. official who explained the Taiwan weapons decision.

WHAT: A big military welcome, two meetings, and a planned State Dinner, where the leaders discussed trade, technology, Taiwan, and Iran, kept their trade truce, and began a new U.S.-China AI Dialogue.
WHERE: At the White House in Washington, D.C., starting with a military welcome on the South Lawn.
WHY: Both sides want stability — keeping things calm between the world's two biggest powers — even though the hard disagreements are not settled.

perspectives.description: Both governments say the visit was friendly and useful: they kept their trade truce, opened talks about keeping AI safe, and both say they want stability.
Some people would say this is mostly talk. There were no new rules on AI, and the Taiwan weapons question was handled quietly, so the hardest problems are still waiting.

Analysts see the meetings as small steps. Keeping the trade truce and starting an AI Dialogue are real agreements, but trade, Taiwan, and technology will need many more meetings before they are solved.
